kinds:
A short reflection on the mystery, often with a prayer at the end. The words come from preachers and the Church's great teachers. Read it once, then keep it in mind through the ten Hail Marys.

St. Alphonsus Liguori · Venerable Fulton J. Sheen · St. John Henry Newman · St. Thomas Aquinas

Longer passages that place you within the mystery: what was seen, heard, and felt there. Read slowly. You do not need to finish the page before the ten Hail Marys end.

Blessed Anne Catherine Emmerich · Venerable Mary of Agreda · St. Ignatius of Loyola · Fr. Frederick William Faber

Meditations written by saints. They also appear under their other kind.

St. Alphonsus's, for example, are under both Saints and Reflections.

The Scripture passage for the mystery, then a few lines of meditation on it.

The Seven Sorrows are set this way, because the Gospel tells the whole scene. For a verse on every bead, open any of the mysteries and choose The Scriptural Rosary, above the meditations.
forms: Every prayer is said aloud. Pray along with the voice.
The meditation is read aloud. You say the prayers.
Every verse and prayer is said aloud.
A verse is shown for each Hail Mary. You read and pray in silence.
The beads are on the screen. Swipe for each Hail Mary.
Count on your own rosary. The screen shows one mystery at a time.
forms_pages: A voice leads every prayer, with no readings between.
One verse of Scripture for every Hail Mary.

The beads move with the voice — for praying with the phone put away, or for learning the prayers by ear. Each mystery, a scene from the lives of Jesus and Mary, is announced, and each prayer is shown on the screen as it is said. Pause the voice to pray quietly for a while.

Each mystery, a scene from the lives of Jesus and Mary, is told verse by verse. The Our Father bead names the mystery and a grace to ask for, each of the Hail Marys has its own verse, and the Glory Be closes it.
forms_listing: A Bible verse for every Hail Mary
